title: Sardis (Revelation 3:1–6)
hook: you have a name for being alive, but wake up

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thyatira: a church whose latest works were more than its first. Your line was more than at first. What did you do one notch better? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-four.

A cliff so steep that the guards didn't bother watching it. That's the story the old Greek historian Herodotus tells about the citadel of Sardis: an enemy soldier saw a defender climb down the rock to fetch a fallen helmet, noticed the way up that nobody was guarding, and the city fell. Some readers hear that old story behind today's letter. Others say the letter needs no backstory at all. Either way, its opening line lands like an alarm going off. The risen Christ says to the church in Sardis: everyone thinks you're alive. You aren't. Wake up.

First, the verdict, in the King James words: "I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead." A name for being alive. A good reputation, a full calendar, people who'd say this church is thriving. Notice what's missing. No persecution is named. No false teacher. Just a church that has fallen asleep inside its own good name. Second, what to do about it: "Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die." Not start over. Strengthen what remains. Like a fire that's nearly out: you don't build a new one, you blow on the embers that are still red. Then: "Remember therefore how thou hast received and heard, and hold fast, and repent." Go back to how it began. Third, the warning: "If therefore thou shalt not watch, I will come on thee as a thief, and thou shalt not know what hour I will come upon thee." It echoes Jesus in the Gospels: "Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come." A thief doesn't send a calendar invite. Fourth, and this is the tender part: "Thou hast a few names even in Sardis which have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with me in white." Even in a sleeping church, some are awake, and the letter counts them: a few names. And the promise to whoever overcomes is that their name will not be blotted out of the book of life. So Sardis sets two names side by side: the name a church has with everyone else, and the name kept in the book of life. The letter cares about the second.

Here's the practice: wake up to one thing. Settle, and breathe. Then choose something right around you that you've stopped noticing. The sound of the room. The weight of your own hands. The light on a wall. Look at it, or listen to it, as if you'd never met it before. When your mind drifts back to sleep, and it will, just notice, and wake up to it again. That's all watchfulness is, one return at a time. If you pray, you can ask to be kept awake. If you don't, just keep returning. The bell holds the time.
Sardis. The church with a name for being alive, told to wake up and strengthen what remains, with a few in white who never fell asleep.
Your line: wake up. Today, pick one thing you usually do on autopilot, and do it once with your full attention, start to finish. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Christians use the language of watchfulness and waking up in sermons and prayers, and some churches read the Gospel warnings to keep watch in Advent.

original.note: Greek: to stay awake, to keep watch. behind 'be watchful' in Revelation 3:2.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sardis is a scolding for a bad church.
what it means: a church with a good name had fallen asleep, and is told to wake up and strengthen what's left.
what a scholar hears: Herodotus tells how the citadel of Sardis fell where no one kept watch; some readers hear that behind 'I will come on thee as a thief.'
